updates.summary: A binding treaty under which Parties must ensure that activities within the lifecycle of AI systems are consistent with human rights, democracy and the rule of law. It requires measures on transparency and oversight, including identification of AI-generated content, accountability, equality, privacy, reliability and safe innovation; remedies, procedural safeguards and notice of interacting with an AI system; and a graduated framework to identify, assess and mitigate risks, with testing where appropriate and possible bans or moratoria. It applies to public authorities; for private actors, each Party declares how it addresses risks. National defence is excluded.
updates.notes: Adopted by the Council of Europe Committee of Ministers on 17 May 2024 and opened for signature in Vilnius on 5 September 2024; the English and French texts are equally authentic. Under Article 30 it enters into force on the first day of the month after a three-month period following the date on which five signatories, at least three of them Council of Europe member States, have consented to be bound. The EU signed on 5 September 2024 and approved the Convention by Council Decision (EU) 2026/1080 of 21 April 2026, after the European Parliament's consent of 11 March 2026; the text was published in the EU Official Journal on 13 May 2026 (OJ L, 2026/1081), and the EU declared that it applies the Convention to private actors through the AI Act. EUR-Lex gives the date of entry into force as unknown (pending notification) or not yet in force. Parties need not apply it to activities protecting their national security interests. A Conference of the Parties follows its implementation, and each Party reports to it within two years of becoming a Party.

updates.summary: Public summary of NATO's revised AI strategy, which updates the 2021 strategy as generative AI and frontier or foundation models spread. It calls for an Alliance-wide AI testing, evaluation, verification and validation (TEV&V) landscape, standards and review tools for responsible adoption, and testing facilities that check whether AI applications can be used safely.

The published text is a summary of the strategy. NATO's members include the United States and Canada, although the record's region is Europe.

updates.summary: Proposed directive that would have set common rules for non-contractual, fault-based civil claims for damage caused by AI systems. National courts could order providers or users of a high-risk AI system suspected of causing damage to disclose evidence, and would presume non-compliance with a duty of care where a defendant failed to do so. Courts would also presume a causal link between the defendant's fault and the AI system's output under set conditions; for providers of high-risk systems, fault meant breaching AI Act requirements on training data, transparency, human oversight, accuracy, robustness or cybersecurity. Both presumptions were rebuttable.
updates.notes: Proposed on 28 September 2022 (COM(2022) 496 final, procedure 2022/0303(COD)). updates.official_identifier: C/2024/1459 (OJ C series); Commission document C/2024/390
updates.summary: Establishes the European Artificial Intelligence Office within the Commission's Directorate-General for Communication Networks, Content and Technology to implement and enforce the AI Act. Its tasks include developing tools, methodologies and benchmarks to evaluate general-purpose AI models, in particular very large models with systemic risks; monitoring unforeseen risks from such models, including alerts from the scientific panel; investigating possible infringements; supporting the rules on prohibited practices and high-risk systems; providing the AI Board's secretariat and facilitating codes of practice; and contributing to international cooperation on AI.
updates.notes: Adopted on 24 January 2024 and published in the Official Journal C series on 14 February 2024; it entered into force on 21 February 2024 (Article 9). It was adopted ahead of the AI Act, after the co-legislators' political agreement of 8 December 2023, so that preparation of the Act's implementation could start, and it says it may be revised once the Regulation is adopted. The Office's officials come from the Directorate-General's staff and its operational expenditure from the Digital Europe Programme's specific objective on AI. It is not a European Office within the meaning of the Financial Regulation. As of September 2026 the Office has more than 125 staff in six units, among them unit A3 'AI Safety', and two advisers, a Lead Scientific Adviser and an International Affairs Adviser. Under the powers the AI Act gives the Commission it enforces the rules for general-purpose AI models: it can evaluate models, request information and measures from providers and, in case of infringement, restrict a model's public availability and issue direct fines.

updates.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 June 2024 laying down harmonised rules on artificial intelligence and amending Regulations (EC) No 300/2008, (EU) No 167/2013, (EU) No 168/2013, (EU) 2018/858, (EU) 2018/1139 and (EU) 2019/2144 and Directives 2014/90/EU, (EU) 2016/797 and (EU) 2020/1828 (Artificial Intelligence Act)
updates.summary: Lays down harmonised rules for placing on the market, putting into service and using AI systems in the EU, to protect health, safety and fundamental rights. It prohibits certain AI practices; sets requirements for high-risk AI systems, among them risk management, data governance, record-keeping, human oversight, accuracy and robustness; and imposes transparency duties for chatbots, deepfakes and machine-readable marking of AI-generated content. Providers of general-purpose AI models must document them; providers of models with systemic risk must also evaluate them, including adversarial testing, mitigate systemic risks and report serious incidents.
updates.notes: Adopted on 13 June 2024 and published in the Official Journal (OJ L, 2024/1689) on 12 July 2024; it entered into force on 1 August 2024, the twentieth day after publication. Article 113 as adopted set the application dates: 2 February 2025 for Chapters I and II (general provisions, including AI literacy, and the prohibited practices); 2 August 2025 for notified bodies, general-purpose AI models, governance and penalties, except the fines on providers of general-purpose AI models (Article 101); 2 August 2026 for the rest; and 2 August 2027 for Article 6(1) high-risk systems. Under Article 111, general-purpose AI models placed on the market before 2 August 2025 must comply by 2 August 2027, and AI systems in the large-scale IT systems of Annex X by 31 December 2030. Since 2 August 2026 the AI Office and national authorities enforce the Act; the AI Office holds the enforcement powers over general-purpose AI models. The AI Omnibus, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 of 8 July 2026 (EU-18), published in the Official Journal on 24 July 2026 and in force since 27 July 2026, amended the Act: the high-risk rules now apply from 2 December 2027 for the Annex III use cases and from 2 August 2028 for AI systems in products covered by Annex I; a ninth prohibition, in Article 5(1)(ba) and (bb), of AI systems that generate non-consensual sexually explicit and intimate content or child sexual abuse material, applies from 2 December 2026; generative AI systems placed on the market before 2 August 2026 must meet the Article 50(2) marking duty by 2 December 2026; each Member State must have a national AI regulatory sandbox operational by 2 August 2027; Article 4 now requires providers and deployers to take measures to support AI literacy; the AI Office's oversight of AI systems built on general-purpose AI models is centralised; simplified requirements for SMEs are extended to small mid-cap companies; and access to regulatory sandboxes, including an EU-level sandbox, is widened. EUR-Lex holds a consolidated version of 27 July 2026.

updates.summary: Replaces the 1985 Product Liability Directive with no-fault liability rules under which software, including AI systems, is a product and integrated digital services are covered. Manufacturers stay liable for defects due to software updates or upgrades, missing safety updates or substantial modifications within their control, and defectiveness is assessed taking into account a product's ability to keep learning after it is placed on the market. Defendants can be required to disclose relevant evidence, and courts presume defectiveness or causation where technical or scientific complexity makes them excessively difficult to prove and the claimant shows they are likely.
updates.notes: Adopted on 23 October 2024 and published in the Official Journal (OJ L, 2024/2853) on 18 November 2024; it entered into force on 8 December 2024, the twentieth day after publication. Member States must transpose it by 9 December 2026. It applies to products placed on the market or put into service after 9 December 2026; Directive 85/374/EEC is repealed with effect from that date but continues to apply to products placed on the market or put into service before it. The Commission's product liability page says the Directive applies to products placed on the market as of 9 December 2026. The Commission is to evaluate the Directive by 9 December 2030 and every five years after.

updates.summary: A Commission implementing decision requesting CEN and Cenelec to draft harmonised standards and European standardisation deliverables supporting the AI Act's requirements for high-risk AI systems in Articles 9 to 15, 17 and 43. The standards cover ten areas: risk management, governance and quality of datasets, record keeping, transparency, human oversight, accuracy, robustness, cybersecurity, quality management and conformity assessment. High-risk AI systems that conform to harmonised standards referenced in the Official Journal are presumed to meet the requirements those standards cover. The standards must conform with Union law on fundamental rights and data protection.
updates.notes: It repeals and replaces Implementing Decision C(2023) 3215 of 22 May 2023, which was based on the Commission's proposal for the AI Act: the new request reflects the final text of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 and sets a new deadline because CEN and Cenelec reported significant delays in September 2024, while the scope and technical content of the requested standards stay as in the 2023 request. CEN and Cenelec were to draft the standards and deliver their final report by 31 August 2025, update their work programme and report to the Commission every three months. The decision is addressed to CEN and Cenelec, ceases to apply if they do not accept the request, and expires on 28 February 2027. Applying the resulting standards remains voluntary. CEN and Cenelec work on them in Joint Technical Committee JTC 21; prEN 18286, a quality management system standard for AI Act purposes supporting Article 17, became the first harmonised standard for AI to enter public enquiry, on 30 October 2025. Under the request CEN and Cenelec completed the harmonised standard on quality management systems for providers of AI systems, including post-market monitoring (point 9 of Annex I), as EN 18286:2026; Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2026/2274 of 12 October 2026 published its reference in the Official Journal on 14 October 2026, from when compliance with it gives a presumption of conformity.

updates.summary: A Commission communication on the risks and opportunities of advanced AI for cybersecurity: AI can help detect vulnerabilities and prevent attacks, but it can be misused to automate attacks and find weaknesses at unprecedented speed and scale. To promote the safe use of advanced AI, the Commission will strengthen EU capacity to evaluate AI models before they are placed on the market, in line with the AI Act, with third-party assessment of capabilities and risks that supports the AI Office; define with ENISA a European blueprint for structured access to advanced AI for cybersecurity; and create with ENISA and the JRC a secure platform to test AI for critical sectors.
updates.notes: Adopted at Strasbourg on 7 July 2026 and sent to the Council on 8 July 2026 (Council document 11711/26). The plan has three objectives: promoting the safe and responsible use of advanced AI, reinforcing the EU's cybersecurity and resilience, and scaling up Europe's AI capabilities for cybersecurity; the communication sets them out as three pillars, followed by work with like-minded partners. It promotes the implementation of the NIS2 Directive and the Cyber Resilience Act, encourages organisations to use AI, including open-source models, to find and fix vulnerabilities, and has ENISA provide guidance and a campaign to secure critical open source software. The Commission will launch an EU Grand Challenge on AI for cybersecurity. Its nine key actions include the EU evaluation capacity for AI models (2027), the access Blueprint and the testing platform (Q4 2026), ENISA guidance on protection against AI-powered threats (from Q3 2026), a pilot Critical Open Source Resilience Campaign (Q4 2026), the Grand Challenge (Q4 2026) and training modules for cybersecurity professionals (Q4 2026). The Blueprint will not introduce new obligations for providers, the evaluation capacity will not be a conformity assessment body, and the testing platform is for testing AI for cyber resilience, not for evaluating general-purpose AI models for compliance with the AI Act. The Commission will set up a working group with ENISA, the European Defence Agency and the Member States on the security risks of frontier AI in defence and dual-use critical systems. Internationally, it will work in the G7 and the UN, with the Network of Advanced AI Measurement, Evaluation and Science, and with NATO, and it will regularly assess the plan's implementation. The plan builds on the AI Act, the Cyber Resilience Act, the NIS2 Directive, the Digital Operational Resilience Act and the Cyber Solidarity Act.

updates.summary: Amends the AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) to simplify its implementation. It moves the application of the high-risk rules from 2 August 2026 to 2 December 2027 for Annex III systems and 2 August 2028 for systems covered by Annex I product legislation, and adds prohibitions, applying from 2 December 2026, on AI systems that generate non-consensual intimate or sexually explicit material of identifiable people or child sexual abuse material. It makes the AI Office exclusively competent for AI systems built on a provider's own general-purpose AI models and for AI in very large online platforms and search engines, and extends measures for SMEs to small mid-cap enterprises.
updates.notes: Commission proposal COM(2025) 836 final of 19 November 2025 (procedure 2025/0359(COD)), part of the digital omnibus package. As proposed, the high-risk rules would have applied 6 months (Annex III) or 12 months (Annex I) after a Commission decision confirming that support measures such as harmonised standards were available, and in any case by 2 December 2027 and 2 August 2028; generative AI systems already on the market would have had until 2 February 2027 to meet the Article 50(2) marking obligation. The adopted text fixes the high-risk dates and sets 2 December 2026 for marking. The European Parliament adopted its position on 16 June 2026 and the Council its decision on 29 June 2026; the act was signed at Strasbourg on 8 July 2026, published in the Official Journal (OJ L, 2026/1744) on 24 July 2026 and entered into force on 27 July 2026, the third day after publication. Dates set by the amendments: the new prohibitions in Article 5(1), points (ba) and (bb), apply from 2 December 2026; providers of generative AI systems placed on the market before 2 August 2026 must meet the Article 50(2) marking obligation by 2 December 2026; each Member State must have at least one national AI regulatory sandbox operational by 2 August 2027; the high-risk rules of Chapter III, Sections 1 to 3, apply from 2 December 2027 for Annex III systems and from 2 August 2028 for Annex I systems. The AI Office's exclusive competence for systems based on general-purpose AI models excludes AI systems related to Annex I products, systems in point 2 of Annex III, systems of law enforcement and border management authorities and financial institutions that fall under Article 74(6), and systems used in the administration of justice. The regulation also simplifies registration in the EU database of systems that providers assess as not high-risk under Article 6(3), allows processing of special categories of personal data for bias detection and correction where strictly necessary, lets the AI Office set up an AI regulatory sandbox at Union level, and extends real-world testing to high-risk systems covered by Annex I legislation. Machinery moves from Section A to Section B of Annex I, and the Commission is to adopt delegated acts adding AI requirements to the Machinery Regulation (EU) 2023/1230, applying by 2 August 2028. It also amends Regulation (EU) 2018/1139 on civil aviation.
